<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yuankai Luo
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Woping Chen
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tong Liang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Baiqiao Wang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zhenguo Li<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:zhenguol@gmail.com">zhenguol@gmail.com</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, leveraging large-scale pre-training to achieve strong performance. The field has rapidly evolved with additional spatial priors and diverse architectural innovations. However, these advancements are often accompanied by varying training recipes and implementation details, which can make it challenging to disentangle the precise source of empirical gains. In this work, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SimVLA</span>, a streamlined baseline designed to establish a transparent reference point for VLA research. By strictly decoupling perception from control—using a standard vision-language backbone and a lightweight action head—and standardizing critical training dynamics, we demonstrate that a minimal design can achieve state-of-the-art performance. Despite having only 0.5B parameters, SimVLA outperforms multi-billion-parameter models on standard simulation benchmarks without robot pretraining. SimVLA also reaches on-par real-robot performance compared to <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math>. Our results establish SimVLA as a robust, reproducible baseline that enables clear attribution of empirical gains to future architectural innovations.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Frontier Robotics</p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18224v1/real1.jpg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/362;" width="476" height="362" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Out-of-box real-robot task examples.<span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We deploy SimVLA without any additional fine-tuning on our held-out scenes and evaluate it on a set of multi-stage tasks that require both dexterous manipulation and semantic understanding.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The field of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) learning has advanced rapidly, driven by a wave of architectural innovations. Recent methods have proposed increasingly sophisticated designs, ranging from mechanisms that enrich perception with temporal context, to modules that inject explicit 3D spatial awareness, to high-capacity decoders that model complex action distributions. While these contributions have pushed the boundaries of robot capabilities, they also introduce a significant challenge for the research community: attributing performance gains to specific components. Since architectural changes are frequently introduced alongside confounding variables—such as varying pretraining datasets, differing backbone scales, or ad-hoc optimization schedules—it can be difficult to disentangle the impact of a novel mechanism from the underlying training recipe.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To facilitate clearer comparisons and accelerate progress, we introduce <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SimVLA</span>, a streamlined baseline designed to serve as a transparent reference point for VLA research. Our goal is not to suggest that architectural complexity is unnecessary, but to establish a high-performance “lower bound” of complexity against which future innovations can be measured. By providing a clean, minimal design that achieves state-of-the-art results, we hope to help the community better quantify the true added value of sophisticated architectural components when they are introduced.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">SimVLA adopts a modular philosophy that decouples perception from control: a standard pretrained vision-language backbone produces fused representations, which are then processed by a lightweight action head to predict continuous actions. This design offers a critical advantage in future-proofing: as vision-language models (VLMs) evolve, SimVLA allows researchers to swap in the latest SOTA backbones (e.g., upgrading from a 0.5B to a 7B model) without redesigning complex cross-modal adapters. Furthermore, we rigorously standardize the often-overlooked training dynamics—such as data shuffling strategies, action space normalization, and optimization schedules—demonstrating that these implementation details often outweigh architectural differences in their impact on performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Despite its simplicity, SimVLA is both effective and highly efficient. Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> illustrates SimVLA’s zero-shot scene generalization capability when deployed on the Galaxea R1 Lite, additional details about the robot platform and training data are provided in Section <a href="#S4.SS1.SSS2" title="4.1.2 Real-robot (Galaxea R1 Lite) ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1.2</span></a>. Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> further presents a representative example in which our model outperforms multi-billion-parameter baselines while maintaining a compact memory footprint.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S1.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.T1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Performance and efficiency summary.<span id="S1.T1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We report LIBERO success (%) and peak training VRAM at Batch=8 (GB) under a matched evaluation setup.</span></span></figcaption>

<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Our main contributions are:</span></p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SimVLA</span>, a modular VLA baseline that decouples perception from control, enabling a flexible and future-proof design that can easily adapt to new vision-language backbones.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We identify and standardize the “silent” drivers of VLA performance—specifically data shuffling, normalization, and optimization dynamics—providing a rigorous training recipe that enables fair cross-model comparisons.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that this minimal design achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing larger and more complex models on simulation benchmarks while enabling efficient real-robot transfer with zero-shot scene generalization.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The rest of our paper is organized as follows: <a href="#S2" title="2 Related Work ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reviews recent VLA advances. <a href="#S3" title="3 SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> introduces SimVLA and our standardized training recipe. <a href="#S4" title="4 Evaluation ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> evaluates SimVLA in simulation and on real robots with detailed ablations. We draw our conclusion in <a href="#S5" title="5 Conclusion ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The development of VLA models has accelerated rapidly, with numerous approaches proposing diverse strategies to improve robotic control through multimodal learning. In this section, we organize recent advances along three complementary axes: (1) visual and temporal augmentation methods that enrich perceptual inputs with motion cues, predictive modeling, or memory mechanisms; (2) geometric and 3D prior integration that injects explicit spatial understanding into the VLA framework; and (3) complex action representations and architectural innovations that explore more expressive decoders and efficient designs. For a more comprehensive review, readers are encouraged to consult recent surveys <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sapkota et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> that offer systematic analyses of the VLA research landscape.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Visual and Temporal Augmentation.</span>
Early VLA models, such as OpenVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, typically rely on static RGB inputs, which limits their ability to reason about fine-grained physical dynamics or long-horizon dependencies. To bridge this gap, recent approaches have focused on augmenting the visual modality with explicit motion cues or temporal reasoning. For instance, FlowVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, CoT-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and TraceVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> introduce a “visual chain-of-thought” by explicitly predicting optical flow, sub-goal image, or overlaying trajectory traces onto input images, while 4D-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> integrates 4D spatiotemporal information to mitigate state chaos. Additionally, PixelVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> and ReconVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> enhance visual grounding via auxiliary segmentation or reconstruction tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond immediate visual augmentation, several works incorporate predictive modeling to enhance planning. WorldVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and Dream-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> integrate world models to predict future states, while
ThinkAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and IntentionVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> generate plans, or intention descriptions before acting.
To handle long contexts, FPC-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, MemoryVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and HAMLET <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>
propose dedicated memory modules or dual-stream architectures to make history-aware predictions.
While these methods significantly improve state tracking and capture features at multiple temporal scales,
they often incur substantial computational overhead and architectural complexity, requiring auxiliary estimators or multi-stage inference processes that can complicate real-time deployment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Geometric and 3D Priors.</span>
Recognizing that 2D vision-language backbones may lack precise spatial understanding, a growing body of research explicitly injects 3D geometric priors into the VLA framework.
Both 4D-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> and SpatialVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> apply positional encodings to enhance the spatial awareness. 4D-VLA fuses positional encoded 3D coordinates with visual tokens, whereas SpatialVLA introduces ego-centric 3D position encodings that does not rely on camera extrinsics.
GraspVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and MolmoAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>)</cite> both introduce additional spatial priors to enhance chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities.
Specifically, GraspVLA improves 3D awareness in its unified CoT progress through auxiliary training tasks such as detection and target grasp pose estimation,
while MolmoAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>)</cite> utilizes depth-aware perception tokens and visual trace to enable reasoning in space.
Other approaches, such as GeoVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, FALCON <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025d</a>)</cite>, and DepthVLA<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2025</a>)</cite> go a step further by processing point clouds, geometric tokens, or depth maps alongside RGB data.
Although these spatially-aware architectures demonstrate superior precision in geometric tasks, they often introduce dependencies on specific sensors or heavy 3D encoders. This can reduce the model’s generality across diverse embodiments compared to RGB-only baselines which are easier to scale and deploy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action Representations and Architectures.</span>
To address the limitations of simple discrete action tokenization, recent work has explored two primary directions: optimizing architectural efficiency and enhancing the expressivity of action distributions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Focusing on efficiency and adaptation, several works modify the underlying architecture or tokenization scheme to reduce computational overhead. For instance, FAST <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pertsch et al., 2025</a>)</cite> employs frequency-domain tokenization to compress trajectories, while PD-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> accelerates inference via parallel decoding. OpenVLA-OFT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2025</a>)</cite> forgoes action tokenization and directly regress continuous actions instead. On the architectural side, VLA-Adapter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> and FLOWER <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Reuss et al., 2025</a>)</cite> introduce lightweight adapters or action head that lowers computational burden, and X-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> utilizes soft prompts for scalable cross-embodiment learning.
Specialized efficient models like NORA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hung et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, SmolVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shukor et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and GR00T-N1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al., 2025</a>)</cite> further optimize performance on specific hardware or humanoid embodiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Parallel to efficiency, a significant body of work has investigated methods to model continuous multimodal distributions. Diffusion-based policies have emerged as a dominant paradigm in this area, with models like Diffusion Policy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, <math id="S2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, <math id="S2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and DD-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. Meanwhile, UnifiedVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> and UniVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> explore unified tokenization and latent action spaces to capture causal dynamics, while UniAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> and VQ-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> learn universal discrete action codebooks with vector quantization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Despite their performance gains, these models often introduce challenges such as increased inference latency (e.g., iterative diffusion steps) or training instability.
Our work offers a counterpoint to this trend. We demonstrate that a <span id="S2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">simple but strong</span> baseline, built on standard flow matching and a validated training recipe, can achieve competitive performance without the need for additional visual cues, spatiotemporal priors, or major architectural change.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As introduced in <a href="#S2" title="2 Related Work ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, recent VLA models have rapidly evolved with increasingly complex architectural components and additional priors.
While these additions often yield empirical improvements, they also complicate fair comparisons across methods, making it difficult to disentangle gains from architectural novelty versus optimization and implementation choices. In this work, we deliberately take a conservative stance. Rather than introducing new architectural components, we ask a more fundamental question: <em id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how strong can a minimal VLA design be when core modeling and training choices are carefully standardized?</em> Our goal is not to diminish the importance of richer inductive biases, but to establish a clean and reproducible baseline that clarifies what performance is achievable without additional architectural complexity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To this end, we propose <span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SimVLA</span>, a simple and modular VLA baseline that decouples perception and control via a lightweight action head conditioned on vision-language representations. Despite its simplicity, SimVLA achieves competitive—and in several cases state-of-the-art—performance across standard benchmarks, while offering substantial improvements in training efficiency and inference throughput. We hope that this baseline can serve as a strong reference point for future work, enabling more precise evaluation of architectural innovations in VLA systems.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Preliminaries</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Problem Formulation.</span> We model the conditional distribution of a future action chunk
<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}=[a_{t},a_{t+1},\dots,a_{t+H-1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}=[a_{t},a_{t+1},\dots,a_{t+H-1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math>
given an observation <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The observation contains the respective multi-view RGB images <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I^{1}_{t},\dots,I^{n}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I^{1}_{t},\dots,I^{n}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the pairing language instruction <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the robot proprioception (state) <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>:
<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}=[I^{1}_{t},\dots,I^{n}_{t},\ell_{t},s_{t}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}=[I^{1}_{t},\dots,I^{n}_{t},\ell_{t},s_{t}]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">VLM Backbone Encoder.</span>
Following the standard late-fusion paradigm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we employ a pretrained VLM <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> to map multi-view RGB observations and the corresponding language instruction into a shared token representation:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{t}=E_{\phi}(I^{1}_{t},\dots,I^{n}_{t},\ell_{t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{t}=E_{\phi}(I^{1}_{t},\dots,I^{n}_{t},\ell_{t}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, we deliberately treat the VLM as a <em id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">perception-language encoder</em>, rather than as an action-generating module. This design choice reflects a principled separation of responsibilities: high-level semantic understanding is handled by the VLM, while continuous control is delegated to a lightweight action head. Such decoupling enables modularity, simplifies inference, and facilitates controlled analysis of downstream action modeling choices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Although the VLM is used in an encoder-only role, it is not frozen by default. We jointly fine-tune the backbone together with the action head, optionally using a short warm-up stage for training stability. This preserves adaptability to the target robotic domain while maintaining a clear architectural boundary between perception-language representation and action generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action Head.</span>
SimVLA uses a vanilla Transformer encoder <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite> as an action head to model action chunks in continuous space. The action head consumes the fused VLM tokens <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, proprioception <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, a timestep embedding, and a noised action chunk, and predicts the corresponding denoising vector.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Flow Matching.</span>
We model continuous action generation using conditional flow matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lipman et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which learns a deterministic vector field that transforms noise into data under the conditioning of the current observation. Compared to discrete autoregressive decoding or stochastic diffusion-based formulations, flow matching offers a lightweight and stable abstraction that is particularly well-suited for continuous control. Concretely, let <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> denote a normalized action chunk and <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)</annotation></semantics></math> denote Gaussian noise. We sample a noise level <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in(0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in(0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> and construct a noised action <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}=t\epsilon+(1-t)x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}=t\epsilon+(1-t)x</annotation></semantics></math>. The action head <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\theta}(x_{t},o_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\theta}(x_{t},o_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> is trained to predict the corresponding denoising vector field using a standard <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> objective:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\left[\|v_{\theta}(x_{t},o_{t},t)-(\epsilon-x)\|_{2}^{2}\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\left[\|v_{\theta}(x_{t},o_{t},t)-(\epsilon-x)\|_{2}^{2}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">We emphasize that our goal is not to capture highly multi-modal action distributions, but rather to provide a simple and reliable mechanism for generating smooth and temporally consistent action chunks. At inference time, we integrate the learned vector field from noise to data using a small number of Euler steps, resulting in efficient and stable action generation suitable for real-time execution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>SimVLA Architecture</h3>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18224v1/fig1.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/241;" width="452" height="241" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">SimVLA overview.<span id="S3.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> SimVLA is a minimal baseline: a VLM encoder produces fused vision-language tokens once per control step, and a lightweight action transformer performs flow-matching denoising to generate a continuous action chunk.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Design Principle.</span>
SimVLA adopts an intentionally minimal architectural design as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 SimVLA Architecture ‣ 3 SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>: a vision-language encoder produces fused representations once per control step, and a lightweight action transformer generates continuous action chunks via flow matching. Our goal is not to introduce new architectural mechanisms, but to establish a clean and neutral baseline that isolates the effects of action modeling and training dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At each timestep, the fused vision-language tokens <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are first obtained from the VLM backbone. We then construct the input sequence to the action head by concatenating projected VLM tokens, a broadcasted proprioceptive state embedding, a sinusoidal time embedding, and the noised action chunk. This unified token sequence is processed by a vanilla Transformer encoder with pure self-attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, without cross-attention, memory modules, or modality-specific routing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rationale.</span>
We intentionally rely on self-attention over concatenated tokens as a neutral information integration mechanism. While more specialized architectures—such as cross-attention bridges or conditional normalization—may offer additional inductive biases, they also introduce confounding factors that complicate fair comparison. By using a single self-attention transformer, SimVLA allows the model to learn modality interactions directly from data, while keeping architectural assumptions minimal.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Practical Advantages.</span>
This design further yields practical benefits for deployment. Since the vision-language backbone is executed only once per control step, all subsequent denoising iterations are handled by the lightweight action head, resulting in reduced latency and improved inference throughput.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Training and Inference Recipe</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A central takeaway of this work is that strong VLA performance can often be achieved through careful standardization of training and inference details, even with minimal architectural design. In practice, we find that several seemingly minor choices can dominate performance differences if left under-specified. Accordingly, we explicitly control and report the following factors across all experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action Representation and Normalization.</span>
We train the flow model in a normalized continuous action space, using per-dimension statistics computed from the training set. Proprioceptive states are normalized when applicable to improve optimizer conditioning. We predict action chunks of horizon <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> and execute them in a receding-horizon manner; we emphasize that the choice of <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> is a major performance knob and must be tuned per benchmark.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Data Handling.</span>
Beyond action chunking, we carefully control data shuffling during training. Since demonstration trajectories exhibit strong temporal correlations, improper shuffling can lead to brittle optimization and poor long-horizon generalization. We find that consistent shuffling is critical for stable training and fair benchmarking.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimization Dynamics.</span>
We systematically sweep learning rates, warm-up schedules, and learning rate schedulers while keeping batch size and total training steps fixed across comparisons. Notably, we observe that learning rate selection alone can overshadow architectural differences if not properly tuned, underscoring the importance of reporting optimization details for reproducibility.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Architecture Configuration.</span>
While SimVLA employs a minimal action head by default, we ablate action transformer scale, VLM backbone choice, and information injection mechanisms (token concatenation, cross-attention, and conditional normalization). We view these variations as implementation choices rather than architectural novelties, and we report them to contextualize performance differences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Inference.</span>
At inference time, SimVLA follows an <em id="S3.SS3.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">encode-once, denoise-in-the-head</em> workflow. Given an observation, the VLM backbone is executed once to obtain fused tokens, after which the lightweight action head performs a small number of Euler integration steps to generate a clean action chunk. The resulting actions are post-processed and executed in a receding-horizon fashion, enabling efficient real-time control.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Evaluation</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To empirically validate the effectiveness of SimVLA, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation across standard simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic settings.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.1 </span>Simulation Benchmarks</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow standard evaluation protocols for each simulation benchmark and keep the comparison settings consistent to support fair and reproducible results.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LIBERO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</span> We utilize all four standard suites: LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-Long, comprising 10 tasks per suite with 500 expert demonstrations each. This serves as our primary testbed to evaluate the model’s long-horizon consistency and generalization performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LIBERO-PRO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</span> To address the memorization issue in current VLA studies, we evaluate on LIBERO-PRO, a robust benchmark that introduces systematic perturbations across four dimensions: object appearance (Obj), spatial layout (Pos), language instructions (Sem), and task goals (Task).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SimplerEnv <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</span> We evaluate on Simpler-Fractal (Google Robot) and Simpler-Bridge (WidowX) to assess the model’s performance in high-fidelity simulated environments. For Simpler-Fractal, we report variant aggregation scores to test the policy’s robustness against diverse scene variations. For Simpler-Bridge, the evaluation focuses on real-to-sim transfer across tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training Setup.</span> Following recent works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, we train a <em id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">single generalist policy</em> on the union of all standard LIBERO datasets (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long). For LIBERO-PRO, we directly evaluate this policy without additional fine-tuning to strictly test zero-shot robustness.
For SimplerEnv, we train our model on the Fractal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brohan et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and BridgeData-V2 datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Walke et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, strictly following the recent work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.
Across all benchmarks, we train directly from a pretrained VLM backbone, without any robotic data pre-training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Critical Hyperparameters.</span> A key finding of our research is that performance is highly sensitive to a small set of training and design choices, which can easily overshadow architectural differences if left under-tuned. To make our comparisons transparent, we summarize the concrete settings we tried:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Data &amp; representation.</span>
We vary the <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">action-chunk horizon</span> <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\in\{10,20,30\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\in\{10,20,30\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We ablate <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">data shuffling</span> (shuffle vs. no shuffle).
We ablate <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">normalization</span> (on/off) for both actions and proprioception; when enabled, we compute per-dimension statistics (mean/std, with robust quantile estimates) on the training set and normalize accordingly.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimization dynamics.</span>
We sweep the <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">learning rate</span> over <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\{5\!\times\!10^{-5},10^{-4},2\!\times\!10^{-4},5\!\times\!10^{-4}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mpadded style="width:0.108em;" width="0.108em"><mo>,</mo></mpadded><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mpadded style="width:0.108em;" width="0.108em"><mo>,</mo></mpadded><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{5\!\times\!10^{-5},10^{-4},2\!\times\!10^{-4},5\!\times\!10^{-4}\}</annotation></semantics></math>,
<span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">warm-up steps</span> over <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{0,1000\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1000</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{0,1000\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">the scheduler</span> over {cosine decay, none}.
For all variants, we keep the training budget fixed (batch size and total steps/epochs); the exact budgets are reported in the appendix.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Architecture configuration.</span>
<span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Action transformer scale:</span> we use two configurations (small vs. large), as in our training scripts, e.g., <math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{768,12,12\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>768</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{768,12,12\}</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>80M params) vs. <math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{1024,24,16\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1024</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1024,24,16\}</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>300M params) for {hidden size, depth, # heads}.
<span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLM backbone:</span> we compare Florence-2 (0.9B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and SmolVLM-0.5B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marafioti et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
<span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Information injection:</span> we compare (i) token concatenation with pure self-attention (default), (ii) cross-attention injection, and (iii) conditional AdaLN.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Detailed hyperparameters are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Datasets and Experimental Details ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines.</span> We compare SimVLA against a spectrum of representative policies, ranging from standard baselines to recent complex architectures: RT-1-X / RT-2-X <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">O’Neill et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, OpenVLA 2024</a>)</cite>, SpatialVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, UnifiedVLA <cite class="ltx_cite </div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Baseline results are either sourced directly from the original papers or reproduced using open-source implementations under the identical input modalities described above.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">

</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.2 </span>Real-robot (Galaxea R1 Lite)</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond simulation, we evaluate zero-shot cross-scene generalization on a real mobile bimanual robot. We train two policies on the 500 hour Galaxea Open-World Dataset collected with the same embodiment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>: (i) our SimVLA initialized from Florence-2, and (ii) a <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> baseline initialized from the publicly released <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> weights. We then deploy both policies in our own held-out scenes without additional fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on eight multi-stage manipulation tasks that emphasize dexterous, fine-grained manipulation under diverse scenes and objects: <em id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">store the dolls</em>, <em id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">arrange eggs</em>, <em id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">put the flowers in the vase</em>, <em id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">put the pen into the pen holder</em>, <em id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">wipe the desktop</em>, <em id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">fold the clothes</em>, <em id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pick up garbage on the ground</em>, and <em id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">open the drawer</em>. For each task, we report task success under a fixed time budget. Additional dataset/robot details and per-task rubrics are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Datasets and Experimental Details ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Simulation Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results on LIBERO.</span> Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1.1 Simulation Benchmarks ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows that SimVLA achieves the highest reported average success rate under our matched setup. Despite using a compact 0.5B backbone, it surpasses large baselines (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math> 4B) like OpenVLA-OFT (97.1%) and MemoryVLA (96.7%), validating the efficacy of our simple, well-tuned architecture. SimVLA achieves near-perfect scores on <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Spatial</span> (99.4%), <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Object</span> (99.8%), and <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Goal</span> (98.2%), ranking first overall. On the challenging <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Long</span> suite, it attains a robust 96.4%, demonstrating strong temporal consistency without explicit memory modules.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Robustness on LIBERO-PRO.</span> Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1.1 Simulation Benchmarks ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents our evaluation on the rigorous LIBERO-PRO benchmark. SimVLA demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization, with superior Semantic robustness and improved Task robustness, while positional robustness remains challenging. While baselines like OpenVLA and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> collapse to near-zero performance on Task-level perturbations (indicating reliance on trajectory memorization), SimVLA reaches 10.0% success on both <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Goal</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Long</span> suites. SimVLA also ranks first across all suites on Semantic robustness (around 98–100% success). In contrast, position robustness is high only on <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Spatial</span> (29.0%) and remains low on <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Object</span>/<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Goal</span>/<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Long</span>, highlighting a key direction for future work.</p>
</div>

<th id="S4.T5.6.1.17.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" colspan="5"><span id="S4.T5.6.1.17.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Tiny Models (<math id="S4.T5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math> 1B)</span></th></tr>
<tr id="S4.T5.6.1.18" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T5.6.1.18.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">X-VLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025b</a>)</cite></th>
<td id="S4.T5.6.1.18.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">85.5</td>
<td id="S4.T5.6.1.18.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">79.8</td>
<td id="S4.T5.6.1.18.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">61.9</td>
<td id="S4.T5.6.1.18.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">75.7</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T5.6.1.19" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#ECECEC;">
<th id="S4.T5.6.1.19.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.T5.6.1.19.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#ECECEC;">SimVLA</span></th>
<td id="S4.T5.6.1.19.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T5.6.1.19.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#ECECEC;">87.4</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.6.1.19.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T5.6.1.19.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#ECECEC;">65.2</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.6.1.19.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.T5.6.1.19.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#ECECEC;">75.9</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.6.1.19.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T5.6.1.19.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#ECECEC;">76.1</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results on WidowX.</span> As detailed in Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Simulation Results ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, SimVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance with an overall average of 95.8%, effectively tying with the heavily pre-trained X-VLA. Despite strictly adhering to a <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">no pre-training</span> protocol, SimVLA matches X-VLA’s average success rate and even secures perfect scores (100%) on the <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Put Spoon on Towel</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Put Eggplant in Basket</span> tasks. This result is particularly significant as SimVLA outperforms large-scale baselines by substantial margins—surpassing MemoryVLA (71.9%) and FPC-VLA (64.6%).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results on Google Robot.</span> In the Google Robot variant aggregation tasks shown in Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.2 Simulation Results ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, SimVLA achieves an average success rate of 76.1%, outperforming strong baselines such as SpatialVLA (67.5%), RT-2-X (65.6%), and ThinkAct (65.1%). SimVLA is also slightly higher than X-VLA (75.7%) on the overall average. Together, these results suggest that a simple, data-efficient baseline can remain competitive on challenging benchmarks without relying on extensive robotic pre-training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Ablation Studies</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To examine which parts of our training recipe matter in practice (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Training and Inference Recipe ‣ 3 SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>), we conduct controlled ablations on LIBERO by varying one knob at a time while keeping the remaining settings fixed (Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>). Overall, we find that several implementation details are indispensable: changing a single knob can lead to a substantial performance drop, often larger than the gains attributed to architectural changes.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.T6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Ablations on LIBERO.<span id="S4.T6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Each row corresponds to one ablation setting with the remaining knobs fixed to the default configuration.</span></span></figcaption>

<td id="S4.T6.6.1.19.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T6.6.1.19.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">99.2</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.6.1.19.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T6.6.1.19.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">98.0</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.6.1.19.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T6.6.1.19.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">93.8</span></td>
<td id="S4.T6.6.1.19.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T6.6.1.19.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">97.7</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Key Findings.</span>
Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> highlights a few dominant knobs that largely determine performance.</p>
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Data shuffling and normalization are critical.</span>
Disabling either shuffling or action normalization causes a near-collapse in performance, suggesting that stable optimization and consistent action scaling are prerequisites for a strong baseline.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimization dynamics dominate.</span>
The learning rate must be tuned: too large (<math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>) degrades sharply, while too small (<math id="S4.I2.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>) also underperforms.
Likewise, removing the small VLM learning-rate multiplier (setting it to 1.0) hurts substantially, indicating that preserving the pretrained backbone while adapting the action head is important for stable end-to-end training.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Some architecture choices matter, but are secondary to the above.</span>
Scaling down the action head (large<math id="S4.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math>small) only slightly reduces performance, whereas alternative conditioning mechanisms (AdaLN / cross-attention) are noticeably worse than simple token concatenation under our setup.
Switching the VLM backbone to Florence-2 remains competitive, consistent with the modular “VLM encoder + action head” design.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Real-robot Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the following section, we report real-robot evaluation results on Galaxea R1 Lite under the zero-shot, cross-scene protocol described above. We compare our SimVLA against a <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> baseline on eight tasks: <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">store the dolls</em>, <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">arrange eggs</em>, <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">put the flowers in the vase</em>, <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">put the pen into the pen holder</em>, <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">wipe the desktop</em>, <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">fold the clothes</em>, <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pick up garbage on the ground</em>, and <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">open the drawer</em>. Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows example out-of-box deployments of SimVLA in our held-out real-world scenes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results on Real Robot.</span>
Overall, SimVLA achieves performance that is broadly comparable to <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> under the same zero-shot protocol (Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Real-robot Results ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Beyond <em id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">fold the clothes</em>, <em id="S4.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">put the pen into the pen holder</em> and <em id="S4.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">put the flowers in the vase</em>, which remain challenging, the other tasks are typically around 80% success. Notably, our SimVLA is trained end-to-end directly from a pretrained VLM backbone (without any VLA/robot-data pre-training), whereas the <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0.5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0.5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0.5}</annotation></semantics></math> baseline uses its publicly released initialization.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18224v1/galaxea_zero_shot.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/193;" width="476" height="193" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Real-robot zero-shot results on Galaxea R1 Lite.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduced <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SimVLA</span>, a minimalist VLA baseline designed to address the challenge of performance attribution in the rapidly evolving VLA landscape. By strictly decoupling perception from control and adhering to a standardized training recipe, we demonstrated that a small backbone can rival or even outperform multi-billion-parameter SOTA baselines. Our extensive evaluations on the simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks confirm that SimVLA achieves superior performance and scene generalization while maintaining a low memory footprint.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Crucially, our findings highlight that “silent” implementation details—such as data shuffling strategies, action normalization, and optimization dynamics—are often as influential as architectural novelties. By isolating these factors, SimVLA provides the community with a reproducible reference point. We hope that this baseline enables researchers to more rigorously quantify the added value of future architectural innovations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work advances research on Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation by providing a transparent and reproducible baseline. By standardizing training dynamics and simplifying architectural design, our work may facilitate fairer comparisons and more reliable scientific progress in embodied AI research.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Potential positive impacts include improved accessibility to robotic manipulation systems, more efficient deployment of assistive robots in domestic or industrial settings, and reduced computational overhead compared to larger models.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">At the same time, advances in general-purpose robotic manipulation may introduce societal risks, including unintended automation of human labor, misuse in unsafe environments, or deployment without adequate safety validation. We emphasize that SimVLA is evaluated in controlled research settings, and real-world deployment should incorporate appropriate safety constraints, human oversight, and domain-specific validation.</p>
</div>
</section>
